opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that talk stuck with me. What I took away is that Russ was very honest about where things stand. The large behavior model work at TRI is impressive: diffusion policies trained on lots of teleoperated demonstrations, doing dexterous manipulation that would have been really hard to hand-engineer a few years ago. But he was careful not to overclaim what "generalization" actually means.

The big point for me was that we don't really have rigorous ways to measure it yet. You train a policy on a set of tasks, test it on something a bit different, and it either works or it doesn't. But how far out of distribution was that test? Was it a new object, a new scene, or a new task? Without careful evaluation, with enough trials and real statistics instead of a few cherry-picked videos, it's hard to say whether pre-training on more diverse data actually helps, or by how much. I think he showed that multi-task pre-training does help, especially for fine-tuning on new tasks with less data, but the gains are more modest and nuanced than the hype suggests.

Coming from the reinforcement learning and locomotion side, that resonated with me. In locomotion we got robust generalization mostly from massive simulation and domain randomization: the policy sees millions of variations of terrain, friction, and masses, so the real world is just another sample. In manipulation with imitation learning, you're bottlenecked by human demonstrations, so you can't brute-force diversity the same way. That's why I think the interesting question is how to combine the two: use demonstrations or large pre-trained models to get the behaviors bootstrapped, then use simulation and RL to make them robust and push beyond what the demonstrations covered.

So my takeaway was a healthy dose of scientific skepticism. The scaling story might be real for robotics, but we need better evaluation to actually know, and we shouldn't assume data from teleoperation alone will get us all the way there.

r001.rationale: The response says it is hard to determine whether more diverse pretraining improves generalization or by how much, and describes the gains as modest and nuanced.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I was at that talk, and it was a pretty exciting one for me, honestly. The thing that stuck with me most was this idea that they're really starting to see signs of generalization in the policies, and in a way that I think a lot of us in the field had been skeptical about for a while.

So the context is that TRI has been training these large diffusion-policy-style models on a lot of teleoperated manipulation data, across many tasks and many objects. And the big question has always been: okay, you collect data for task A and task B, does that help you with task C? Or are you just memorizing demonstrations? And what Russ was showing was that as they scale the number of tasks and the diversity of the data, they're starting to see behaviors that aren't explicitly in the training set. Things like the robot recovering from a perturbation it never saw, or handling an object that's visually quite different from what it was trained on, or composing little skills in a way that wasn't demonstrated directly.

And what I found refreshing is that he was very careful about it. He wasn't claiming "we've solved generalization." He was framing it more as, here's the evidence, here's where it works, here's where it breaks, and here's how we're trying to evaluate it rigorously. Because evaluation is really the hard part. In simulation, in my world, you can run thousands of rollouts and get clean statistics. In real-world manipulation, each evaluation is a human resetting a scene, and you can fool yourself very easily. So the emphasis on building out systematic evaluation, with held-out objects and held-out conditions, I thought that was the mature part of the talk.

The other takeaway for me, coming from the locomotion and sim-to-real side, is that it reinforced this picture where data diversity matters more than almost anything else. In RL for legged robots we get that diversity through domain randomization and massively parallel simulation. They're getting it through scale of real demonstrations. Different mechanisms, but the underlying lesson is the same: the policy generalizes roughly to the extent that your training distribution forces it to. And I think the interesting question going forward is how you combine those two. Can you use simulation to multiply the diversity of a relatively small set of real demonstrations, and get the best of both? That's where I think a lot of the action is going to be in the next couple of years.

r001.rationale: The response links broader, more diverse training data to generalization and notes limits in evaluating it, but does not express uncertainty about how much of the observed generalization is caused by that broader training.

astra-6.text: What stood out to me was the question of what we actually mean by generalization. A policy might handle a new object or a different arrangement of the scene, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it can perform a new task. Those are quite different capabilities. I’d be cautious about attributing a specific result to Russ’s talk without the details in front of me, but that distinction is what I’d focus on: what changed between training and testing, and how much of the underlying behavior was already represented in the training data?

r001.rationale: The response questions how much behavior was already represented in the training data, but does not express uncertainty about whether broader training with more data explains the observed generalization.

sol-6.1.text: My takeaway was that generalization is still very hard to pin down. If a policy succeeds in a new situation, is it applying something general, or is that situation sufficiently similar to what it saw during training? For robot policies, I think we need to be much more precise about what changed—the object, the environment, the task—and where performance starts to break down. I don’t have enough detail from that particular talk to fairly characterize Russ’s results.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether success reflects generalization or similarity to training situations, but does not mention broader training or more data as a possible source of the observed generalization.
